extracted.intended_audience: geometers, mathematicians, and historians of mathematics (readers interested in porisms, conic sections, and classical constructions)
extracted.subtask_description: Historical and technical survey of methods for inscribing polygons in circles and general conic sections (porisms), comparing geometric, projective and coordinate constructions and evaluating their rigour, generality, and handling of special/indeterminate cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and directness of construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction should be 'remarkably simple and direct' (as praised for Mr. Lowry's construction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer constructions that minimize auxiliary steps and appeal directly to known properties; a simple direct construction is judged favourably. Explicit constructions that are compact and transparent are especially valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and treatment of special/degenerate cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The account should not omit special cases — 'No notice however is taken of special cases: more particularly of that, when the circle is reduced to a point situated in the same line with the other three.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must identify and explicitly treat degenerate or limiting cases (e.g. circle reduced to a point, collinear data) rather than asserting a single-form solution applies universally. Failure to discuss such cases is a substantive omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of established propositions for proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs may legitimately 'appeal for the proof to Stewart's Prop.' or other classical propositions, but such appeals should be explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking standard propositions, cite them and make clear how they apply. Reliance on known results is acceptable, but the dependence should be transparent so the reader can verify the step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unjustified generalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present a generalised statement as proved when the analysis does not support extension — 'There is nothing in the structure of the analysis itself that suggests the investigation to be adapted to the higher values of n.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a method or solution is stated generally, provide explicit demonstration for the general case; otherwise mark the generalisation as conjectural. Distinguish conjecture from demonstrated theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibit invariants and analytic clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer analyses that reveal invariant quantities or fixed magnitudes (example: 'a variable chord of the circle through a determinate point ... is fixed in magnitude but unlimited in position — and therefore that that determinate point is the centre of the circle').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight invariants and structural insights that explain why a construction works; an analysis that gives conceptual understanding (not just manipulations) is judged superior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use projective principles to generalize circle results to conics
rubrics_metrics.description: By 'the adoption of the projective principle, the conic section generally might be substituted for the circle in the enunciation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, apply projective transformations/principles to reduce or generalize problems between circles and conic sections; make the mapping and its consequences explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical elegance and rigour of demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrations are commended when 'exceedingly elegant and strictly geometrical.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek proofs that combine clarity, brevity, and accuracy; elegance (aesthetic simplicity) is a positive criterion but must not sacrifice rigour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and proper attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of priority or borrowing must be handled carefully — the text rebukes unfounded accusations of plagiarism and stresses correct attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document sources, acknowledge prior discoveries, and avoid making or repeating unsupported charges of plagiarism. If similarity to earlier work exists, state the relationship clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider coordinate (Cartesian) methods as valid alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordinate solutions (e.g. 'Mr. Hearn's solution may be considered as purely coordinate') are legitimate and can effectively solve cases where synthetic methods are cumbersome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Cartesian/analytic methods where they simplify derivations; present the algebraic reduction clearly and show how it corresponds to geometric data when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide geometric demonstrations for propositions invoked
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not invoke propositions without proof when readers lack access — 'I had objected to his use of the proposition ... except he gave a geometrical demonstration of it; and he furnished me with one rigidly so.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either supply a proof (geometric or analytic) for non-elementary lemmas used in the main argument or provide clear references; avoid black-box appeals to results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful handling of indeterminate and ambiguous cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguous or indeterminate cases 'require great delicacy and discrimination in their discussion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify conditions that make the problem indeterminate or impossible, classify the types of indeterminacy (e.g. multiple, double, triple indeterminacy), and treat them with careful case analysis rather than sweeping statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show algebraic 'reproductive' character and elimination steps when generalising
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'reproductive character of the equations' and successive elimination of unknowns is an important analytical feature leading to general conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using algebraic methods, exhibit the elimination process and explain how the structure of the equations reproduces the general pattern (this supports conclusions about arbitrary n or general conics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit pole-polar / reciprocal polar relationships where applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of 'reciprocal polars' and pole-polar properties is useful and may be 'directly brought into play' for inscription problems beyond the triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use projective notions (pole/polar reciprocity) to simplify constructions and proofs involving conic sections; make the polar relationships explicit in the construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a method to find points of contact and use them in construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The method should furnish 'the mode of finding those points of contact, nor, of course, the mode of employing them in the construction' (criticised when absent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete steps to locate tangency/contact points and show how to use them in the desired construction; procedural completeness is required for a construction to be fully satisfactory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough literature search and impartial historical representation
rubrics_metrics.description: The author stresses having 'bestown adequate care in the examination of those books' and wishes to 'appreciate and to represent the labours ... with strict impartiality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before asserting priority or completeness, perform a comprehensive literature review and present earlier contributions impartially; note possible gaps and invite later correction if sources were unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include pedagogical examples and exercises where useful
rubrics_metrics.description: The text notes 'They are not difficult — and may form a good exercise for geometrical students.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, add worked examples or exercises to illustrate methods and to make results accessible to students and instructors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag and correct errata in source material
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources may be 'vitiated by several errata, which the reader must correct as he proceeds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out known errata in referenced works and, if possible, provide corrected formulations to prevent propagation of mistakes.
